tool.name: CSS
tool.tagline: The style sheet language that lays out and styles every web page
tool.description: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls how HTML looks: colours, typography, spacing, layout, responsiveness and animation. Modern CSS has flexbox, grid, container queries, custom properties, cascade layers and nesting, so most layouts need no framework and no JavaScript. Every front-end developer, and anyone who builds web pages, needs it.

concepts.name: Rules, declarations and linking CSS
concepts.summary: A CSS rule is a selector plus declarations; attach styles with a linked stylesheet, a style element or inline styles.
concepts.why: Everything in CSS is written as rules, so reading and placing them correctly comes first.
concepts.body:
A stylesheet is a list of **rules**. Each rule has a **selector** that picks elements and a block of **declarations**, each a `property: value;` pair. ```css h1 { color: navy; font-size: 2rem; } ``` There are three ways to apply CSS to a page: - **External stylesheet**: `` in the head. The normal choice: one file, cached by the browser, shared by every page. - **Style element**: `` in the head, handy for small demos or critical CSS inlined for speed. - **Inline style**: `

`. It applies to one element and beats almost every stylesheet rule, so it's hard to override. Avoid it except for values set by JavaScript. Browsers are forgiving: a declaration with an unknown property or invalid value is **dropped** silently and the rest of the rule still applies. That's how newer features can be used with fallbacks, by writing the old value first and the new one second. It also means typos fail quietly, so the browser's devtools are essential: the Styles panel shows invalid declarations struck through with a warning icon. Comments are `/* ... */`; there are no `//` line comments in CSS. **At-rules** start with `@`, such as `@media`, `@import`, `@font-face` and `@layer`, and configure how and when other rules apply.
takeaways: A rule = selector + { property: value; } declarations
Prefer external stylesheets; avoid inline styles
Invalid declarations are dropped silently: check devtools
pitfalls: Writing // comments, which break the following rule.

quiz.q: A rule contains 'color: blu; font-weight: bold;'. What happens?
options: The page fails to load the stylesheet
The color declaration is dropped, bold still applies
The color falls back to blue
quiz.explain: Only the invalid declaration is discarded; valid ones in the same rule still apply.

concepts.name: Selectors and combinators
concepts.summary: Target elements by type, class, id and attribute, and by their position in the tree with descendant, child and sibling combinators.
concepts.why: Precise selectors are how you style exactly the elements you mean and nothing else.
concepts.body:
Selectors choose which elements a rule applies to.

**Simple selectors**:

- type: `p`, `button`
- class: `.card` (any element with `class="card"`; elements can have many classes)
- id: `#main` (unique on the page; avoid for styling because it's very specific)
- attribute: `[disabled]`, `[type="email"]`, `[href^="https"]` (starts with), `[href$=".pdf"]` (ends with)
- universal: `*`

Chain them with no space to require all at once: `button.primary[disabled]` is a disabled button that also has class primary.

**Combinators** select by relationship:

- `nav a` (space): an `a` anywhere inside a `nav` (descendant).
- `ul > li`: an `li` that is a direct child of a `ul`.
- `h2 + p`: the `p` immediately after an `h2` (adjacent sibling).
- `h2 ~ p`: every `p` sibling after an `h2` (general sibling).

A comma makes a **selector list**: `h1, h2, h3 { ... }` applies to all three.

Browsers match selectors right to left: for `.sidebar a` they look at every `a` and then check for a `.sidebar` ancestor. That's fast in practice, so write selectors for clarity. The bigger risk is fragility: long chains like `main div > ul li a` break when the markup changes. Prefer short selectors built around classes that describe what a component is.
concepts.code:
/*
Home Docs
*/ .menu a { text-decoration: none; } /* descendant */ .menu > a { padding: 4px 8px; } /* direct child */ a[href$=".pdf"]::after { content: " (PDF)"; } /* attribute: ends with */ h2 + p { margin-top: 0; } /* first p right after an h2 */ input[type="checkbox"] { accent-color: teal; } button.primary { background: royalblue; color: white; } /* both at once */ button .icon { width: 1em; } /* .icon INSIDE a button */
takeaways: Class selectors are the workhorse; avoid ids for styling
space = descendant, > = child, + = next sibling, ~ = later siblings
No space means 'same element': a.b is different from a .b
pitfalls: Writing 'button .primary' (descendant) when you meant 'button.primary' (same element).

quiz.q:
Which elements does 'ul > li' match in
  • A
    1. B
?
quiz.explain: > requires a direct parent ul; B's parent is an ol.

concepts.name: Cascade, specificity and inheritance
concepts.summary: Learn how the browser picks a winner when several rules set the same property, and which properties children inherit.
concepts.why: Most 'my CSS doesn't work' moments are the cascade doing exactly what it's specified to do.
concepts.body:
When several declarations set the same property on an element, the **cascade** decides which wins, checking in order:

- **Origin and importance**: author styles beat browser defaults; `!important` declarations beat normal ones.
- **Cascade layers** (`@layer`): later layers beat earlier ones; covered in an advanced lesson.
- **Specificity**: the more specific selector wins.
- **Order**: if all else is equal, the declaration that comes last wins.

**Specificity** is compared as three numbers (A, B, C): A counts ids, B counts classes, attributes and pseudo-classes, C counts type selectors and pseudo-elements. `#nav .link` is (1,1,0) and beats `.menu .link:hover` at (0,3,0), because one id outranks any number of classes. Inline `style` attributes beat any selector. The universal selector `*` and combinators add nothing.

**Inheritance** is separate: some properties, mostly text-related ones like `color`, `font-family`, `font-size`, `line-height` and `visibility`, pass from parent to child automatically. Box properties like `margin`, `border`, `width` and `background` don't. Any property can be forced with the keywords `inherit`, `initial`, `unset` or `revert`.

An inherited value always loses to any rule that targets the element directly, however unspecific. That's why `body { color: gray }` doesn't color links: the browser stylesheet targets `a` directly.

Treat `!important` as a last resort. It escalates fights instead of ending them; keep specificity low and flat instead.
concepts.code:
/*

Hello link

*/ p { color: black; } /* (0,0,1) */ .lead { color: green; } /* (0,1,0) beats p */ #intro { color: purple; } /* (1,0,0) beats .lead -> text is purple */ p.lead { color: orange; } /* (0,1,1) still loses to the id */ body { font-family: Georgia, serif; } /* inherited by p and a */ .lead { border: 1px solid; } /* NOT inherited by the link */ a { color: inherit; } /* opt in: link takes the p's purple */
takeaways: Order of checks: importance, layer, specificity, then source order
Specificity = (ids, classes/attrs/pseudo-classes, types)
Text properties inherit; box properties don't
A direct rule always beats an inherited value
pitfalls: Reaching for !important instead of fixing specificity.

quiz.q: Which wins for color: '.card .title' (two classes) or '#hero h2' (id + type)?
options: Whichever comes last in the file
They combine into a mixed colour
'#hero h2', one id outranks any number of classes
quiz.explain: Specificity compares ids first: (1,0,1) beats (0,2,0).

concepts.name: Colours, units and values
concepts.summary: Write colours in hex, rgb, hsl and oklch, and choose between px, rem, em, %, vw and other units for sizes.
concepts.why: Picking the right unit is the difference between a layout that scales with user settings and one that breaks.
concepts.body:
**Colours** can be written several ways:

- Keywords: `red`, `rebeccapurple`, `transparent`, `currentColor` (the element's text colour).
- Hex: `#1e90ff`, with alpha `#1e90ff80`.
- `rgb(30 144 255 / 50%)` and `hsl(210 100% 56%)`, in the modern space-separated syntax.
- `oklch(65% 0.2 250)`: lightness, chroma, hue. It's perceptually uniform, so equal lightness steps look equal, which makes palettes easy. All current browsers support it.

**Lengths** come in two families.

- Absolute: `px` is the practical one (a reference pixel, not a device pixel).
- Relative: `rem` is relative to the root font size (16px by default, and user-adjustable), `em` to the element's own font size (for font-size itself, the parent's), `%` to the parent's corresponding dimension, `vw`/`vh` to 1% of the viewport width/height, and `ch` to the width of a "0".

A good default: `rem` for font sizes and most spacing, so everything scales when a user raises their browser's font size; `px` for borders and hairlines; `%` or `fr` for layout widths. `em` compounds when nested, which is handy for padding that scales with a button's own text, but confusing for font sizes in nested lists.

On phones, `100vh` can be taller than the visible area because of browser toolbars. Use `100dvh` (dynamic viewport height) or `100svh` (smallest) instead.

`calc()` mixes units: `calc(100% - 2rem)`.
takeaways: rem for type and spacing, px for borders
oklch gives perceptually even colours
Use dvh/svh instead of vh for full-height mobile layouts
calc() mixes units
pitfalls: Setting html { font-size: 62.5% } tricks or px-only fonts that ignore the user's preferred text size.

quiz.q: With the default root font size, .box { font-size: 20px; padding: 2em; } has how much padding?
quiz.explain: em on padding is relative to the element's own font size: 2 x 20px.

concepts.name: The box model
concepts.summary: Every element is a box of content, padding, border and margin; box-sizing decides whether width includes padding and border.
concepts.why: Spacing and sizing bugs almost always come from misunderstanding how these four layers add up.
takeaways: content + padding + border + margin
box-sizing: border-box makes width include padding and border
margin-inline: auto centers a block with a width
Vertical margins between blocks collapse to the larger one
pitfalls: Adding padding to a width: 100% element with content-box and getting a horizontal scrollbar.

quiz.q: With box-sizing: content-box, width: 200px, padding: 10px, border: 2px, what is the rendered width?
quiz.explain: 200 content + 2 x 10 padding + 2 x 2 border = 224px.

concepts.name: Display and normal flow
concepts.summary: Control how a box takes part in layout with display: block, inline, inline-block, none, and understand normal flow.
concepts.why: Normal flow is the default layout every other technique builds on or breaks out of.
concepts.body:
Without any layout CSS, elements are arranged by **normal flow**: block boxes stack vertically, each taking the full available width; inline boxes sit side by side in lines of text and wrap like words.

The `display` property changes how a box takes part:

- `block`: new line, full width, respects width/height and vertical margins.
- `inline`: flows in text. `width` and `height` are ignored, and vertical padding and margins don't push other lines away.
- `inline-block`: flows in text like a word but is sized like a block, which suits buttons and badges.
- `none`: removes the element from layout and from the accessibility tree.
- `flex` and `grid`: the element becomes a container that lays out its children; later lessons cover both.

`display` really has two parts: the **outer** type (how the box behaves with siblings: block or inline) and the **inner** type (how it lays out its children: flow, flex, grid). That's why `inline-flex` exists, an inline-level box whose children are a flex layout.

Hiding elements has options with different effects:

- `display: none`: no space, not rendered, hidden from screen readers.
- `visibility: hidden`: invisible but still takes up space.
- `opacity: 0`: invisible, takes space, still clickable and focusable.

To hide something visually but keep it for screen readers, use a "visually hidden" utility class (clip-path plus a 1px size), not `display: none`.
takeaways: Normal flow: blocks stack, inline boxes wrap in lines
Inline boxes ignore width and height; inline-block doesn't
display: none removes from layout and accessibility; visibility: hidden keeps space
pitfalls: Setting width on a span and wondering why nothing changes.

quiz.q: Which hides an element but keeps its space in the layout?
quiz.explain: visibility: hidden makes the box invisible while it still occupies space.

concepts.name: Typography and web fonts
concepts.summary: Style text with font-family stacks, size, weight, line-height and spacing, and load custom fonts efficiently with @font-face.
concepts.why: Text is most of what users read; good type settings matter more for readability than any other styling.
concepts.body:
Most of a page is text, and a handful of properties control it.

- `font-family` takes a **stack**: `"Inter", system-ui, sans-serif`. The browser uses the first available font, and the generic family at the end is the final fallback. `system-ui` uses the operating system's interface font, which looks native and loads instantly.
- `font-size` in `rem`; `font-weight` from 100 to 900 (400 normal, 700 bold); `font-style: italic`.
- `line-height` unitless, around 1.4 to 1.6 for body text. Unitless values are multiplied by each element's own font size; a value like `24px` would be inherited as a fixed size and squash larger headings.
- `letter-spacing`, `text-transform`, `text-align`, `text-decoration`.
- `max-width: 65ch` keeps lines readable.

**Web fonts** are declared with `@font-face`, giving a family name, a `src` URL (use WOFF2, the compressed standard format) and the weights and styles the file covers. A **variable font** covers a whole weight range in one file: `font-weight: 100 900`.

`font-display: swap` shows fallback text immediately and swaps in the web font when it loads, instead of hiding text for up to three seconds. Self-host fonts or preload the critical one, and limit yourself to a couple of families and weights; each file is a separate download.

`clamp()` gives fluid type: `font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 1rem + 2vw, 2.5rem)` grows with the viewport between a minimum and maximum. Keeping a `rem` term in the middle value means it still responds to user zoom.
takeaways: Always end a font stack with a generic family
Use unitless line-height
WOFF2 + font-display: swap for web fonts
clamp() gives fluid sizes with limits
pitfalls: Setting line-height in px on body, so big headings inherit a cramped fixed line height.

quiz.q: Why is line-height: 1.5 usually better than line-height: 24px on body?
options: The unitless factor is recomputed for each element's own font size
quiz.explain: Children inherit the factor, not a fixed length, so big text gets proportionally larger line height.

concepts.name: Backgrounds, borders and shadows
concepts.summary: Decorate boxes with background colours, images and gradients, rounded borders, outlines and shadows.
concepts.why: These are the everyday properties that turn plain boxes into buttons, cards and banners.
concepts.body: **Backgrounds** paint behind the content and padding. - `background-color` and `background-image`, which can be a `url()` or a **gradient**: `linear-gradient(to right, #6366f1, #ec4899)`, `radial-gradient(...)` or `conic-gradient(...)`. - `background-size: cover` fills the box, cropping as needed; `contain` fits the whole image. - `background-position: center` and `background-repeat: no-repeat` control placement. - Several backgrounds can be layered, separated by commas, with the first on top. **Borders**: `border: 1px solid #ddd` is shorthand for width, style and colour; individual sides use `border-top` or the logical `border-block-start`. `border-radius` rounds corners: `8px` for cards, `50%` for a circle on a square, `999px` for a pill. **Outline** looks like a border but takes no space and doesn't affect layout, which is why browsers use it for focus rings. `outline-offset` moves it out from the edge. **Shadows**: `box-shadow: 0 4px 12px rgb(0 0 0 / 15%)` takes x offset, y offset, blur, optional spread and colour. Add `inset` for inner shadows and separate several shadows with commas for more realistic depth. `text-shadow` does the same for text, and `filter: drop-shadow()` follows the shape of transparent images. Images that convey content belong in HTML `` with alt text; CSS backgrounds are for decoration only, because screen readers can't see them.
takeaways: Gradients are background images; layers are comma-separated, first on top
border-radius: 50% makes a circle
outline doesn't affect layout, which suits focus rings
Meaningful images go in HTML, decoration in CSS
pitfalls: Removing focus outlines for looks without providing a visible :focus-visible style.

quiz.q: In background: url(a.png), url(b.png), which image is drawn on top?
options: Only the last one is used
quiz.explain: The first background layer listed is painted on top.

concepts.name: Flexbox
concepts.summary: Lay items out in a row or column with flexbox, distributing space and aligning them with justify-content, align-items and gap.
concepts.why: Flexbox handles navbars, toolbars, centering and card rows: most one-dimensional layout on the web.
concepts.body:
`display: flex` turns an element into a **flex container** and its direct children into **flex items**, laid out along one axis.

- `flex-direction: row` (default) or `column` sets the **main axis**. The other is the cross axis.
- `justify-content` distributes items along the main axis: `flex-start`, `center`, `space-between`, `space-around`, `space-evenly`.
- `align-items` aligns them on the cross axis: `stretch` (default, equal heights), `center`, `flex-start`, `baseline`.
- `gap: 1rem` puts space between items without margin tricks.
- `flex-wrap: wrap` lets items wrap onto new lines instead of shrinking.

Each item's size is controlled with the `flex` shorthand, `flex: grow shrink basis`:

- `flex: 1` means grow to share free space equally (basis 0).
- `flex: none` keeps the content size, neither growing nor shrinking.
- `flex: 0 0 200px` makes a fixed 200px column.

Two classic patterns: perfect centering with `display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center`, and pushing one item to the far end with `margin-left: auto`, since auto margins absorb free space.

Remember that justify-content works on the main axis, so it becomes vertical when `flex-direction: column`. And flexbox is one-dimensional: when you need rows *and* columns to line up, use grid.
takeaways: justify-content = main axis, align-items = cross axis
gap spaces items; flex-wrap allows new lines
flex: 1 shares free space; flex: none keeps content size
margin-left: auto pushes an item to the end
pitfalls: Expecting justify-content to center vertically in a flex-direction: column container; there it's align-items for horizontal.

quiz.q: In a flex-direction: column container, which property centers items horizontally?
quiz.explain: With a column direction the cross axis is horizontal, and align-items works on the cross axis.

concepts.name: Pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements
concepts.summary: Style elements by state or position with pseudo-classes like :hover and :nth-child, and generate content with ::before and ::after.
concepts.why: Interactive states and structural styling are impossible without them, and they replace lots of extra markup.
concepts.body:
**Pseudo-classes** (one colon) select elements in a particular state or position.

- User action: `:hover`, `:active`, `:focus`, and `:focus-visible`, which matches only when the browser decides a focus ring should be shown (keyboard focus, not mouse clicks). Use it for focus styles.
- Form state: `:checked`, `:disabled`, `:required`, `:invalid`, `:user-invalid`, `:placeholder-shown`.
- Structure: `:first-child`, `:last-child`, `:only-child`, `:nth-child(2n+1)` (odd items), `:nth-child(3)`, `:nth-of-type()`, `:empty`.
- Negation: `:not(.active)`.
- Links: `:link` and `:visited` (for privacy, only colours can change on visited links).

**Pseudo-elements** (two colons) style a part of an element or create a box that isn't in the HTML.

- `::before` and `::after` insert a generated child at the start or end. They require the `content` property, even if it's just `content: ""`, and they don't exist on void elements like `img` and `input`.
- `::first-line`, `::first-letter`, `::placeholder`, `::selection`, `::marker` (list bullets), `::backdrop` (behind a modal dialog).

Generated content is decoration. Screen readers may or may not read it, and users can't select it, so never put essential information in `content`.

A useful recipe: `li:not(:last-child)` adds separators between items without a trailing one.
takeaways: Pseudo-classes = state/position (:hover); pseudo-elements = parts (::before)
Use :focus-visible for focus rings
::before/::after need a content property
Generated content is decoration, not information
pitfalls: Forgetting content: "" so ::before never appears.

quiz.q: Which selector matches the 1st, 3rd, 5th... items of a list?
quiz.explain: odd is the same as 2n+1, matching positions 1, 3, 5 and so on.

concepts.name: Positioning
concepts.summary: Move boxes out of normal flow with relative, absolute, fixed and sticky positioning and the inset properties.
concepts.why: Badges, dropdowns, sticky headers and overlays all depend on positioning and on finding the right containing block.
concepts.body:
`position` decides how `top`, `right`, `bottom`, `left` (or the shorthand `inset`) are applied.

- `static` (default): normal flow; inset properties do nothing.
- `relative`: stays in flow, but is shifted visually by the offsets. Its original space is kept. Mostly used as an anchor for absolutely positioned children.
- `absolute`: taken out of flow (siblings close the gap) and positioned relative to its **containing block**: the nearest ancestor whose position isn't static. If none exists, the initial containing block (the viewport-sized area at the top of the page) is used.
- `fixed`: positioned relative to the viewport; it stays put when the page scrolls. (An ancestor with a `transform` or `filter` becomes its containing block instead, a famous gotcha.)
- `sticky`: behaves like relative until scrolling would move it past its offset, e.g. `top: 0`, then sticks within its parent's bounds.

The common pattern for a badge on a card: parent `position: relative`, child `position: absolute; top: 8px; right: 8px`. `inset: 0` on an absolute child covers the parent completely, which is ideal for overlays.

When sticky doesn't stick, the cause is almost always an ancestor with `overflow: hidden` or `auto` (sticky then sticks inside that scroll box), or a parent no taller than the sticky element itself.

Positioned elements can overlap; `z-index` orders them, covered in the stacking context lesson.
takeaways: absolute is relative to the nearest positioned ancestor
relative keeps the original space; absolute removes it
sticky needs an offset (top: 0) and breaks inside overflow ancestors
inset: 0 fills the containing block
pitfalls: A sticky header that never sticks because an ancestor has overflow: hidden.

quiz.q: An absolutely positioned child has top: 0; right: 0, but its parent is position: static. What is it positioned against?
options: The viewport, and it stays fixed while scrolling
The nearest ancestor with non-static position, or the initial containing block
quiz.explain: Only positioned ancestors form a containing block for absolute positioning.

concepts.name: CSS Grid
concepts.summary: Build two-dimensional layouts with grid-template-columns, fr units, repeat, minmax, auto-fit and named areas.
concepts.why: Grid makes page layouts, galleries and dashboards that used to need frameworks a few lines of CSS.
concepts.body:
`display: grid` lays children out in rows and columns at once.

**Defining tracks**: `grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr 1fr` makes three columns. The `fr` unit takes a fraction of the remaining free space. `repeat(3, 1fr)` is three equal columns, and `minmax(200px, 1fr)` is a track that's at least 200px and grows to share space. Rows are created automatically as needed; `grid-auto-rows` sizes them. `gap` spaces rows and columns.

The responsive-gallery one-liner needs no media queries: `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(220px, 1fr))` fits as many 220px+ columns as there's room for, and stretches them to fill the row.

**Placing items**: by default items fill cells in order. To place explicitly, use line numbers: `grid-column: 1 / 3` spans from line 1 to line 3, or `grid-column: span 2`. Negative numbers count from the end, so `1 / -1` spans the full width.

**Named areas** make page layouts readable:

```css
grid-template-areas: "head head" "side main" "foot foot";
```

then `grid-area: main` on a child. Changing the template in a media query rearranges the whole layout.

Alignment works like flexbox: `justify-items`/`align-items` within cells, and `place-items: center` for both. Choose grid when you think in rows *and* columns, flexbox when content in one line should decide its own size.
takeaways: fr shares free space; minmax() sets a range
repeat(auto-fit, minmax(X, 1fr)) is a responsive grid with no media queries
grid-column: 1 / -1 spans the full width
Named areas make layouts readable and easy to rearrange
pitfalls: Using grid-column: 1 / 3 and expecting it to span three columns; it spans lines 1 to 3, two columns.

quiz.q: grid-template-columns: 100px 1fr 2fr in a 400px wide container with no gap. How wide is the last column?
quiz.explain: 300px is free after the fixed column; 2fr of 3fr total is 200px.

concepts.name: Sizing, overflow and aspect ratio
concepts.summary: Control box sizes with min/max constraints, min(), max(), clamp(), aspect-ratio and object-fit, and handle content that overflows.
concepts.why: Real content is unpredictable; constraints instead of fixed sizes keep layouts intact with long words and odd images.
concepts.body: Fixed `width` and `height` break as soon as content changes. Constrain instead: - `max-width: 100%` stops images overflowing their container; `min-height` lets a box grow with its content instead of clipping it. - `width: min(100%, 60rem)` picks the smaller of two values, a one-line responsive container. `max()` picks the larger; `clamp(min, preferred, max)` combines both. - `aspect-ratio: 16 / 9` gives a box a ratio, with the height computed from the width. Great for video embeds and card images. - `object-fit: cover` makes an `` fill its box, cropping instead of stretching; `object-position` picks the focal point. When content is bigger than its box, `overflow` decides what happens: `visible` (default, spills out), `hidden` (clipped), `auto` (scrollbars only when needed), `scroll` (always) and `clip` (like hidden, but doesn't create a scroll container). `overflow-x` and `overflow-y` set each axis. Long unbroken strings like URLs overflow narrow boxes. `overflow-wrap: anywhere` lets them break. For a single line with an ellipsis, combine `white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis`. For several lines, use `line-clamp`, available today as `-webkit-line-clamp` together with `display: -webkit-box` and `-webkit-box-orient: vertical`. `scrollbar-gutter: stable` reserves space for a scrollbar so content doesn't shift when one appears.
takeaways: Prefer min/max constraints to fixed sizes
min(), max() and clamp() compute responsive sizes
aspect-ratio + object-fit: cover for consistent media boxes
text-overflow: ellipsis needs nowrap and overflow: hidden
pitfalls: Setting a fixed height on a text container, which clips or overflows when the text grows.

quiz.q: What does width: min(100%, 600px) produce on a 400px-wide container?
quiz.explain: min() picks the smaller value: 100% of 400px is 400px.

concepts.name: Custom properties (CSS variables)
concepts.summary: Define reusable values with --name and read them with var(), with cascading, inheritance and fallbacks, to build themes.
concepts.why: Variables make design tokens, theming and dark mode a matter of changing a few values.
concepts.body:
A **custom property** is any property whose name starts with `--`. You define it like any declaration and read it with `var()`:

```css
:root { --brand: #4f46e5; }
.button { background: var(--brand); }
```

They're not preprocessor variables: they live in the browser, take part in the cascade and **inherit**. Defining `--brand` on `:root` makes it available everywhere; redefining it on `.danger-zone` changes it for that subtree only. Change one with JavaScript (`el.style.setProperty("--x", "10px")`) and everything using it updates live.

`var(--gap, 1rem)` supplies a fallback used when the variable isn't defined. Fallbacks can nest: `var(--a, var(--b, 4px))`.

Values are stored as token streams and only checked when used. If `--size: red` is used in `width: var(--size)`, the declaration becomes **invalid at computed-value time** and the property falls back to its inherited or initial value, not to an earlier declaration in your stylesheet.

Variables work well as design tokens: colours, spacing scale, radii, fonts. Theming becomes overriding tokens:

- `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root { --bg: #111; --fg: #eee; } }`,
- or a `[data-theme="dark"]` attribute toggled by a script.

Variables can't be used in selectors or media query conditions. To animate one, or make it type-checked, register it with `@property`, covered with animations.
takeaways: --name defines, var(--name, fallback) reads
Custom properties cascade and inherit, so they can be scoped
Theming = redefining tokens under a media query or attribute
Invalid values at use time fall back to inherited/initial, not earlier rules
pitfalls: Expecting var() to work inside a media query condition like @media (min-width: var(--bp)).

quiz.q: --pad is set to 8px on :root and 20px on .card. What padding does a .card .title with padding: var(--pad) get?
quiz.explain: Custom properties inherit, so the title sees the nearest definition: .card's 20px.

concepts.name: Media queries and responsive design
concepts.summary: Adapt layouts to screen size and user preferences with mobile-first media queries, range syntax and preference queries.
concepts.why: Most traffic is mobile; responsive CSS is how one codebase serves every screen.
concepts.body:
**Responsive design** means one page that adapts to any screen. It rests on three things: the viewport meta tag in the HTML, flexible layouts (flexbox, grid, %, `fr`, `min()`), and **media queries** for the changes flexibility can't handle.

A media query applies rules only when a condition is true:

```css
@media (width >= 48rem) { .nav { display: flex; } }
```

The range syntax (`width >= 48rem`, `30rem <= width < 60rem`) is supported in all current browsers and is clearer than the older `min-width`/`max-width` form, which means the same thing.

Write **mobile-first**: base styles for small screens, then `width >=` queries that add complexity as space grows. Small screens get the simplest CSS, and the cascade stays easy to follow. Choose breakpoints where *your content* breaks, not by device models. Using `em`/`rem` in queries makes them respect user font-size settings.

Media queries also detect **user preferences and capabilities**:

- `prefers-color-scheme: dark` for dark mode,
- `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` to tone down animation, which is important for people with vestibular disorders,
- `hover: hover` and `pointer: coarse` to tell mouse users from touch users,
- `print` for print stylesheets.

Many layouts need fewer queries than you'd think: `repeat(auto-fit, minmax())`, `flex-wrap` and `clamp()` adapt continuously. Use media queries for structural changes, like turning a stacked menu into a horizontal bar.
takeaways: Mobile-first: base styles small, add with width >= queries
Pick breakpoints where the content breaks
Respect prefers-reduced-motion and prefers-color-scheme
Flexible layouts reduce the number of queries you need
pitfalls: Desktop-first max-width queries that pile overrides on top of each other.

quiz.q: With mobile-first CSS, where do the styles for the smallest screens go?
options: Outside any media query, as the base styles
In a separate stylesheet loaded by JavaScript
quiz.explain: Mobile-first means the unconditional base is the small-screen layout, enhanced by min-width queries.

concepts.name: Transitions and keyframe animations
concepts.summary: Animate changes between states with transition, and run multi-step animations with @keyframes and the animation property.
concepts.why: Small, purposeful motion makes interfaces feel responsive and shows users what changed.
concepts.body:
**Transitions** animate a property from its old value to its new one when it changes, for example on `:hover` or when a class is toggled:

```css
.button { transition: background-color 150ms ease, transform 150ms ease; }
```

Each entry has a property, duration, optional timing function (`ease`, `linear`, `ease-in-out`, `cubic-bezier()`, `steps()`) and delay. List specific properties rather than `transition: all`, which animates things you didn't intend and costs performance.

Not everything can transition. Discrete properties like `display` historically just flipped. Modern CSS allows `transition-behavior: allow-discrete` together with `@starting-style`, which defines the "before" state for elements that just appeared, so dialogs and popovers can fade in and out.

**Keyframe animations** run on their own, without a state change:

```css
@keyframes spin { to { rotate: 1turn; } }
.loader { animation: spin 1s linear infinite; }
```

The `animation` shorthand sets name, duration, timing function, delay, iteration count (`infinite`), direction (`alternate`) and `fill-mode` (`forwards` keeps the final frame).

For smooth 60fps motion, animate `transform` and `opacity`: the browser can run those on the compositor without recalculating layout. Animating `width`, `top` or `margin` triggers layout every frame and can stutter.

Always honour `prefers-reduced-motion`: replace large movements with fades or nothing.
takeaways: transition animates between states; @keyframes runs a sequence
List specific properties, not transition: all
Animate transform/translate and opacity for smooth motion
@starting-style animates elements as they appear
pitfalls: Animating height or top, which triggers layout on every frame.

quiz.q: Which property change is cheapest for the browser to animate?
quiz.explain: Transforms can be animated on the compositor without layout or paint.

concepts.name: Transforms
concepts.summary: Move, rotate, scale and skew elements visually with transform and the individual translate, rotate and scale properties.
concepts.why: Transforms power hover effects, icons, carousels and smooth animations without disturbing the layout.
concepts.body:
Transforms change how an element is drawn without changing layout: its original box still occupies the same space, and neighbours don't move.

The functions:

- `translate(x, y)` moves it; percentages are relative to the element's own size, so `translate(-50%, -50%)` shifts by half its own width and height.
- `rotate(45deg)` (or `0.25turn`), `scale(1.1)` or `scale(x, y)`, `skew(10deg)`.
- 3D: `rotateY()`, `translateZ()`, `perspective()`.

In the `transform` property, functions apply right to left in terms of coordinate space, so **order matters**: `rotate(45deg) translateX(100px)` moves along the rotated axis, while `translateX(100px) rotate(45deg)` moves right and then rotates in place.

Modern CSS also has the individual properties `translate`, `rotate` and `scale`. They're applied in a fixed order (translate, rotate, scale, then `transform`), and you can change one without repeating the others, which is ideal for transitions and hover states.

`transform-origin` sets the pivot point; the default is the center. `transform-origin: top left` makes a menu scale out from its corner.

Side effects to know: a transform creates a new **stacking context** and becomes the containing block for `position: fixed` descendants, so a fixed element inside a transformed parent stops being fixed to the viewport.
takeaways: Transforms don't affect layout; neighbours stay put
Function order in transform matters
translate, rotate and scale properties can be changed independently
A transform creates a stacking context and traps fixed descendants
pitfalls: Putting a position: fixed modal inside a transformed parent and seeing it scroll with the page.

quiz.q: A box is translated 50px to the right with transform. What happens to the element after it?
options: It moves into the gap left behind
It stays where it was; layout is unchanged
It wraps to the next line
quiz.explain: Transforms are purely visual; the original box keeps its place in layout.

concepts.name: :is(), :where() and :has()
concepts.summary: Group selectors with :is() and zero-specificity :where(), and select parents and earlier siblings with :has().
concepts.why: :has() finally lets CSS style an element based on what it contains, replacing many JavaScript class toggles.
concepts.body:
Three functional pseudo-classes changed how CSS is written.

**:is()** takes a selector list and matches any of them: `:is(h1, h2, h3) a` instead of three selectors. Its specificity is that of its **most specific** argument, so `:is(#id, p)` counts as an id everywhere.

**:where()** works the same way but always has **zero specificity**. It's perfect for defaults and resets that should be easy to override: `:where(ul, ol)[role="list"] { list-style: none; }`.

**:has()** is the long-awaited relational selector. `A:has(B)` matches A if B matches relative to it:

- `.card:has(img)` is a card that contains an image (a "parent selector").
- `h2:has(+ p)` is an h2 immediately followed by a p (look forwards from a sibling).
- `form:has(:user-invalid)` is a form with an invalid field, to disable its submit style.
- `body:has(dialog[open])` locks page scrolling while a modal is open.
- `label:has(input:checked)` styles the label of a checked input.

`:has()` takes the specificity of its most specific argument, like `:is()`, and it can't be nested inside another `:has()`.

Browsers optimise these well, but avoid extremely broad patterns like `*:has(*)` on large documents. With `:has()`, `:is()` and `:where()`, many state classes that JavaScript used to toggle become plain CSS.
takeaways: :is() groups selectors and takes the highest specificity of its arguments
:where() groups with zero specificity
:has() selects an element by its descendants or following siblings
pitfalls: Putting an id inside :is() and accidentally raising the specificity of the whole selector.

quiz.q: What is the specificity of :where(#main .nav) a?
quiz.explain: :where() contributes zero, leaving only the type selector a.

concepts.name: Native CSS nesting
concepts.summary: Write nested rules directly in CSS with & and nested at-rules, without a preprocessor.
concepts.why: Nesting keeps component styles together and removes the main reason many projects used Sass.
concepts.body:
CSS supports nesting natively in every current browser. Inside a rule you can write further rules that apply relative to the parent selector.

```css
.card {
  padding: 1rem;
  & h2 { margin: 0; }          /* .card h2 */
  &:hover { background: #f8f8f8; }  /* .card:hover */
  .dark & { background: #222; }    /* .dark .card */
}
```

`&` stands for the parent selector. A nested selector without `&` is treated as a descendant, so `h2 { }` inside `.card` means `.card h2` (the `&` is optional there). Use `&` explicitly when attaching pseudo-classes (`&:hover`) or when the parent goes in the middle or end (`.dark &`).

Media queries, container queries, `@supports` and `@layer` can nest inside a rule, applying to the current selector, which keeps responsive tweaks next to the styles they modify.

Differences from Sass to know:

- No string concatenation: `&__title` (BEM-style suffixes) does **not** work.
- `&` behaves like `:is(parent)`, so specificity follows `:is()` rules: a parent list such as `#a, .b` is treated as if it were the id everywhere.
- Declarations written after nested rules are allowed; they're treated as if in their original order.

Don't nest deeply. Each level adds specificity and couples styles to markup structure; one or two levels is plenty.
takeaways: & is the parent selector; nested selectors default to descendants
Media and container queries can nest inside rules
No Sass-style &__suffix concatenation
Keep nesting to one or two levels
pitfalls: Porting Sass that relies on &-suffix concatenation and getting silently broken selectors.

quiz.q: Inside .btn { ... }, what does '&.primary' select?
quiz.explain: With no space, & joins the selectors on the same element.

concepts.name: Container queries
concepts.summary: Make components respond to the size of their container rather than the viewport with container-type and @container.
concepts.why: A card that adapts to its slot works in a sidebar, a grid or full width without page-level breakpoints.
concepts.body:
Media queries ask about the viewport, but a component doesn't know where it will be placed: the same card may sit in a narrow sidebar or a wide main column. **Container queries** let it respond to the space it actually has.

Two steps:

- Mark an ancestor as a container: `container-type: inline-size` (query its width). Optionally name it with `container-name: sidebar`, or use the shorthand `container: sidebar / inline-size`.
- Query it: `@container (width >= 30rem) { ... }`. Rules inside apply to descendants of the nearest container that matches (or the named one: `@container sidebar (width >= 30rem)`).

A container can't style itself based on its own size; queries apply to its descendants. And `inline-size` containment means the container's width must not depend on its children, which is normal for blocks and grid cells but not for shrink-to-fit elements. Use `size` only if you also need height queries, because it requires an explicit height.

**Container query units** size things relative to the container: `cqi` is 1% of its inline size, so `font-size: clamp(1rem, 4cqi, 2rem)` gives type that scales with the card.

**Style queries** like `@container style(--variant: compact)` query custom property values on the container (supported in Chromium and Safari; check support before relying on them).

Use media queries for page-level layout and container queries for reusable components.
takeaways: container-type: inline-size makes an element queryable
@container rules apply to descendants, never the container itself
cqi units size relative to the container
Media queries for pages, container queries for components
pitfalls: Querying an element's own size; the query must target an ancestor container.

quiz.q: Why can't an element with container-type: inline-size use @container to change its own width?
options: Queries apply to descendants; restyling the container could create a loop
quiz.explain: Size containment requires the container's size not to depend on what the query changes.

concepts.name: Cascade layers
concepts.summary: Organise styles into @layer groups so whole layers win or lose regardless of specificity, taming resets, libraries and utilities.
concepts.why: Layers end specificity wars between your code, frameworks and third-party CSS.
concepts.body:
**Cascade layers** add a step to the cascade that's checked *before* specificity. Declare the order once:

```css
@layer reset, base, components, utilities;
```

Then put rules into layers with `@layer components { ... }` or `@import url(lib.css) layer(vendor)`. A declaration in a later layer beats one in an earlier layer, **however specific** the earlier selector is. So `.mt-0` in `utilities` beats `#sidebar .card h2` in `components`.

Rules:

- Unlayered styles beat all layered styles (for normal declarations). Wrap third-party CSS in an early layer and it can never accidentally override yours.
- Order is set by the first time a layer name appears, so declare the full order at the very top.
- Layers can nest (`@layer components.buttons`).
- `!important` reverses the order: an important declaration in an *earlier* layer beats one in a later layer, and important layered styles beat important unlayered ones. That lets a reset layer protect critical values.

Within a layer the normal rules still apply: specificity, then source order.

The `revert-layer` keyword rolls a property back to what the previous layers would have given it.

Layers suit design systems well: resets lowest, then base element styles, components, and utilities on top, so single-purpose classes always win without `!important`. Tailwind CSS v4 is built exactly this way.
takeaways: Layer order is checked before specificity
Declare the order up front: @layer a, b, c;
Unlayered styles beat layered ones
!important reverses layer order
pitfalls: Leaving most CSS unlayered and then wondering why layered framework styles never win.

quiz.q: A rule in @layer base uses #id .a (high specificity); a rule in a later layer uses .a. Which wins?
options: The base rule, because of the id
Whichever comes last in the file
Neither; they conflict and both are dropped
quiz.explain: Layer order is compared before specificity, so the later layer wins.

concepts.name: z-index and stacking contexts
concepts.summary: Understand painting order, z-index and the stacking contexts that make a z-index: 9999 still appear behind something.
concepts.why: Overlapping menus, modals and tooltips fail in confusing ways until stacking contexts make sense.
concepts.body:
When boxes overlap, the browser paints them in a defined order. `z-index` changes that order, but only within a **stacking context**.

`z-index` works on positioned elements (any position except static) and on flex and grid items. Higher values paint on top of lower ones *in the same stacking context*.

A **stacking context** is a group that is painted as a unit: its children are layered among themselves, then the whole group is placed in its parent context according to its own z-index. A child can never escape its context. A modal with `z-index: 9999` inside a parent context at `z-index: 1` still sits below a sibling context at `z-index: 2`.

Many properties create a new stacking context, often unintentionally:

- `position` relative/absolute with a `z-index` other than auto; `position: fixed` or `sticky` always,
- `opacity` below 1, `transform`, `filter`, `backdrop-filter`, `mix-blend-mode`,
- `isolation: isolate`, `will-change` for some properties, `contain: paint`, container queries' `container-type`.

Debugging approach: find the nearest ancestors that form stacking contexts and compare *their* z-index values, not the child's.

Good practice: use a small scale of z-index tokens (dropdown 10, sticky 20, modal 30), use `isolation: isolate` on components to contain their internal z-indexes, and for modals and popovers use `dialog` and `popover`, which render in the **top layer** above all stacking contexts.
takeaways: z-index only compares elements within the same stacking context
opacity < 1, transform, filter and more create contexts
Fix layering by adjusting the ancestor context
dialog and popover use the top layer, above everything
pitfalls: Escalating z-index values on a child whose ancestor context is the real problem.

quiz.q: A tooltip has z-index: 1000 but appears under a sibling section. Its parent has opacity: 0.99. Why?
options: The parent forms a stacking context, so the tooltip's z-index only applies inside it
quiz.explain: opacity below 1 creates a stacking context that contains the tooltip.

concepts.name: Organising CSS at scale
concepts.summary: Keep large stylesheets maintainable with naming conventions like BEM, component scoping, @scope, design tokens and utility classes.
concepts.why: CSS is global by default; without structure, every change risks breaking a distant page.
concepts.body:
Every CSS rule is global, so large projects need conventions to stay maintainable. The approaches overlap, and modern codebases mix them.

**Naming conventions.** BEM names classes as block, element and modifier: `.card`, `.card__title`, `.card--featured`. Every selector is a single class, so specificity stays flat, and the names show where a style belongs.

**Scoping.** CSS Modules or framework-scoped styles (Vue, Svelte, Angular) rewrite class names per component. Shadow DOM isolates web components. Native `@scope (.card) to (.card-content) { ... }` limits rules to a subtree with a lower boundary, and **scoping proximity** makes the nearest scope win when two scopes conflict.

**Utility-first.** Frameworks like Tailwind use small single-purpose classes in the markup, which avoids naming and dead CSS at the cost of longer class lists.

**Design tokens.** Spacing, colour and type scales defined once as custom properties keep everything consistent and make theming possible.

**Layers.** `@layer reset, base, components, utilities` sets precedence explicitly.

General rules:

- Keep specificity low and flat: classes, not ids or long chains.
- Style components independently of where they appear; let parents handle layout (gap, grid) instead of children setting outer margins.
- Co-locate styles with components and delete them with the component.
- Lint with Stylelint and let a formatter handle style.
takeaways: Global CSS needs conventions: naming, scoping or utilities
Keep specificity flat with single-class selectors
Tokens + layers give consistency and predictable precedence
@scope limits rules to a subtree, with a lower boundary
pitfalls: Components that set their own outer margins, which breaks them in new contexts.

quiz.q: Why does BEM recommend .card__title over .card h2?
options: Single-class selectors keep specificity flat and decouple styles from markup structure
h2 elements can't be styled with classes
quiz.explain: A unique class avoids specificity growth and survives changes like switching h2 to h3.

concepts.name: Formatting contexts and margin collapsing
concepts.summary: Learn how block and inline formatting contexts work, when margins collapse, and how display: flow-root contains floats.
concepts.why: Strange gaps, escaped margins and collapsed parents all follow from formatting-context rules.
concepts.body:
Layout in CSS is organised into **formatting contexts**: regions where boxes are laid out by one set of rules.

A **block formatting context** (BFC) stacks block boxes vertically. Inside one, vertical margins of adjacent blocks **collapse**: the gap is the larger of the two margins (or the sum of the largest positive and most negative). Collapse also happens between a parent and its first or last child when nothing separates them (no border, padding, inline content or height). That's why a child's `margin-top` can appear *outside* its parent, pushing the parent down.

A new BFC is created by the root, floats, absolutely positioned elements, inline-blocks, table cells, `overflow` other than visible/clip, flex and grid items, and explicitly by **`display: flow-root`**. Margins never collapse across a BFC boundary, and a BFC contains its floats: the classic fix for a parent with zero height because all children float is `display: flow-root`.

An **inline formatting context** lays out text and inline boxes in **line boxes**. Each line's height comes from `line-height` and the tallest inline content aligned by `vertical-align`. Images are inline by default and sit on the text baseline, leaving a small gap underneath for descenders; `display: block` or `vertical-align: middle` removes it.

Flex and grid containers establish their own **flex/grid formatting contexts**, where margins never collapse and floats don't apply. This is one reason spacing with `gap` in flex or grid is more predictable than stacking margins.
takeaways: Vertical margins collapse inside a BFC, including parent/first-child
display: flow-root creates a BFC with no side effects
BFCs contain floats and block margin collapse across their edge
Flex and grid contexts never collapse margins
pitfalls: Adding padding: 1px hacks to stop margin collapse instead of display: flow-root.

quiz.q: A section with no padding or border contains an h1 with margin-top: 40px. Where does the gap appear?
options: Inside the section, above the h1
Nowhere; margins on headings are ignored
Above the section, because the margin collapses through
quiz.explain: With nothing separating them, the child's top margin collapses with the parent's and shows outside it.

concepts.name: The rendering pipeline and performance
concepts.summary: Follow how style, layout, paint and composite turn CSS into pixels, and use that to avoid jank, layout thrashing and costly selectors.
concepts.why: Smooth scrolling and animation depend on knowing which CSS changes are cheap and which redo the whole page.
concepts.body:
After parsing, the browser turns DOM plus CSSOM into pixels in stages:

- **Style**: compute the final value of every property for every element (selector matching, cascade, inheritance).
- **Layout** (reflow): compute each box's size and position.
- **Paint**: record drawing commands for text, colours, borders and shadows, split into layers.
- **Composite**: the GPU combines layers into the final frame.

A change only redoes the stages from where it enters. Changing `width`, `font-size` or `margin` triggers layout, paint and composite. Changing `color` or `background` skips layout. Changing `transform` or `opacity` on an element with its own layer can skip straight to composite, which is why animations should use them.

**Layout thrashing** happens when JavaScript interleaves writes and reads, such as setting a style and then reading `offsetHeight` in a loop. Each read forces a synchronous layout. Batch reads before writes, or use `requestAnimationFrame`.

Tools for containing the cost:

- `will-change: transform` hints that an element will animate so the browser can promote it to a layer ahead of time. Use it sparingly; every layer costs memory.
- `contain: layout paint` (or `content`) promises the subtree doesn't affect outside layout, limiting how much is redone.
- `content-visibility: auto` skips rendering off-screen sections entirely; pair it with `contain-intrinsic-size` to keep scrollbars stable.

Selector matching is rarely the bottleneck today; large DOMs and forced layouts usually are. Profile with the Performance panel, which colours style, layout, paint and composite work separately.
takeaways: Pipeline: style, layout, paint, composite
transform and opacity animations can skip layout and paint
Interleaving style writes and layout reads causes thrashing
content-visibility: auto skips off-screen rendering
pitfalls: Putting will-change on many elements permanently, wasting GPU memory.

quiz.q: Changing which property most likely triggers layout?
quiz.explain: Width changes geometry, so layout, paint and composite all run again.

concepts.name: Modern colour: oklch, color-mix, relative colour
concepts.summary: Use perceptual colour spaces, wide-gamut P3 colours, color-mix() and relative colour syntax to build palettes in pure CSS.
concepts.why: Generating hover states, tints and themes from one brand colour removes hand-maintained colour tables.
concepts.body:
CSS colour has moved well beyond sRGB hex.

**Colour spaces.** `rgb()` and `hsl()` describe sRGB, which is non-perceptual: `hsl(60 100% 50%)` yellow looks far lighter than `hsl(240 100% 50%)` blue at the same "lightness". `oklch(L C H)` and `oklab()` are **perceptually uniform**: equal L means equal perceived lightness, which makes accessible palettes and consistent contrast much easier. `color(display-p3 1 0 0)` and high-chroma oklch values reach **wide-gamut** colours on modern screens. Out-of-gamut colours are mapped to what the display can show, so give an sRGB fallback where precision matters.

**color-mix()** blends two colours in a chosen space: `color-mix(in oklch, var(--brand), white 20%)`. Mixing in oklab or oklch avoids the muddy grey midpoints of sRGB mixing.

**Relative colour syntax** derives a colour from another: `oklch(from var(--brand) calc(l - 0.1) c h)` is a darker brand for hover, and `rgb(from var(--brand) r g b / 50%)` adds transparency. One token generates a whole scale.

**light-dark()** picks a value by the element's `color-scheme`: `color: light-dark(#111, #eee)`, with `color-scheme: light dark` on `:root`.

Interpolation space matters in gradients too: `linear-gradient(in oklch, blue, yellow)` avoids the grey middle that sRGB gradients produce.

Finally, check contrast: perceptual lightness helps, but WCAG contrast ratios must still be checked with tools.
takeaways: oklch is perceptually uniform: equal L looks equally light
color-mix(in oklch, ...) blends without muddy midpoints
Relative colour syntax derives hover and alpha variants from one token
light-dark() + color-scheme for simple theming
pitfalls: Assuming equal hsl lightness means equal perceived lightness or contrast.

quiz.q: What does oklch(from var(--c) l c calc(h + 180)) produce?
options: The complementary hue at the same lightness and chroma
quiz.explain: It keeps l and c and rotates the hue by 180 degrees.

concepts.name: Intrinsic sizing and the flex algorithm
concepts.summary: Master min-content, max-content and fit-content, how flex items grow and shrink, and why min-width: auto causes overflow.
concepts.why: Mysterious overflow in flex and grid layouts is almost always an intrinsic-size rule at work.
concepts.body:
Boxes have **intrinsic sizes** derived from their content:

- `min-content`: the narrowest the box can be without overflowing, roughly its longest word or widest image.
- `max-content`: its width if nothing wrapped.
- `fit-content`: max-content, but capped at the available space (and at least min-content).

These keywords work in `width`, `grid-template-columns` and elsewhere. `width: fit-content` shrink-wraps a block, and `grid-template-columns: max-content 1fr` sizes a label column to its longest label.

**The flex algorithm.** Each item starts at its `flex-basis` (or its width, or content size when the basis is `auto`). Free space is then distributed in proportion to `flex-grow`, or, if space is negative, removed in proportion to `flex-shrink` × basis. That's why `flex: 1` (basis 0) gives equal columns while `flex: auto` (basis auto) gives columns proportional to their content.

**The automatic minimum.** Flex items have `min-width: auto` by default, which resolves to their min-content size. An item containing a long URL, a `<pre>` block or a wide table refuses to shrink below that and overflows the container. The fix is `min-width: 0` on the flex item (or `overflow: hidden`, which also sets the automatic minimum to 0). Grid has the same issue: `1fr` means `minmax(auto, 1fr)`, so use `minmax(0, 1fr)` for tracks that must be able to shrink.

Percentages in heights only resolve when the parent has a definite height; flex and grid stretching usually provide one, which is why `height: 100%` works in some layouts and not others.
takeaways: min-content, max-content and fit-content size boxes from their content
flex: 1 (basis 0) gives equal columns; flex: auto doesn't
Flex items default to min-width: auto; set min-width: 0 to let them shrink
Use minmax(0, 1fr) for grid tracks that must shrink
pitfalls: Debugging flex overflow by adding overflow: hidden on the container instead of min-width: 0 on the item.

quiz.q: A flex: 1 item contains a wide code block and overflows the row. What is the usual fix?
quiz.explain: The automatic minimum size keeps the item at its min-content width; min-width: 0 removes it.
